author: snake_case
text:
Honestly we’ve all been doing this for many years already by hiring contractors to build entire platforms by themselves with very little oversight.

It doesn’t matter what country they’re in, the company makes the decision to hire like 100 contractors to build the thing and like 5 devs to oversee it and the whole project is a massive dumpster fire and somehow makes it to prod anyway and then the company is stuck with it for years until they decide to rewrite it and rinse and repeat.

Now it’s just 5 devs overseeing the AI in those companies that do things like that.

Not all companies do it that way, though. My company hired full time workers in other countries so that devs are always producing code 24 hrs a day and we are definitely dealing with slop, but we were before, and on some teams the AI has actually helped enforce code standards.

The massive issue we’ve having is that it often produces code that looks right, but isn’t. It’s so easy to pass on your own misunderstandings to the agent that sometimes we end up with features that, for example, don’t take into account established scope and permissions requirements. This seems like something that will be solved with time, though.

author: kacey
text:
Ctrl-F didn't turn up any results for "union" and only an off-target hit for "organize". RIP to an entire industry which never learned that, in order to negotiate effectively, you need to come to the bargaining table with leverage (and that leverage evaporates when you become trivially replaceable). Oh well.

Hopefully this is a lesson to every other industry that AI is being forced into. The best time to set up sustainable industries which exclude employer-driven exploitation is yesterday, the next best time is now.

author: skybrian
text:
It's relatively easy to start a new software company compared to other industries and I think software developers with ambition are more likely to do that. Why form a union to fight with management when you can replace management with your own?

And even people who don't want to be management might join a new company with their friends, or just switch companies. The grass is always greener.

author: kacey
text:
It's relatively easy to start a new software company [...]


Relatively easy != easy.


Why form a union to fight with management when you can replace management with your own?


Existing customer base, proven business model, coworkers as a known factor.


And even people who don't want to be management might join a new company with their friends, or just switch companies. The grass is always greener.


Switching companies doesn't change that employers negotiate as a bloc, and employees negotiate as individuals. The mentality of leaving everyone to fend for themselves has gotten us here. For people who're fine with this state of affairs, cool, more power to ya. This blog post examines people who aren't, so my comment is targeted at them, and others who could relate to that situation.

author: raze2012
text: Given the VC's slowly tightening their belts and the horror stories in the job market: we're not currently in a market of "start a new company" or "just switch jobs". It's more a question of if you need to get your foot in the door, hold on for dear life, or just take this chance to leave on an extended sabbatical leveraged by years of savings.

author: Akir
text:
Personally speaking I’ve been viewing this topic as a sister to the vibe-coded adobe suite one, and under that light your response is almost funny. The so much of the world’s capital is dominated by large monolithic legacy tech companies: Adobe, Oracle, Microsoft, Apple, etc.

Moreover, large companies tend to buy out smaller companies in the same industry all the time to increase their market share, so for the people in that company any “freedom” they get from that company’s practices could very easily be temporary. But it likely won’t matter anyways because they won’t unionize in this small company so they won’t have any control over their futures. This is assuming they stay in the same company to begin with instead of simply jumping ship and moving to greener pastures.

It’s not that new tech companies can’t happen obviously, it’s just that the deck is stacked against them and without unionization most of the people are going to be at the whims of a select few.

author: skybrian
text:
Well, working at a startup should probably be considered a temporary job, for maybe a year or two. The company will likely change radically in some way or another. I've worked at startups that failed; it's no fun, but I did get paid. Also got a decent payout when a startup that I used to work got bought out after I left.

That was back in the dot-com era though, and the aftermath. I earned a lot more at Google, and now I'm retired and out of touch.

author: Akir
text:
Isn't that also a bad way of thinking? If you want to be involved in the way things are managed, why would you only want to be part of a temporary job? Pay is only part of the experience, after all. But everyone has different motivations.

I didn't put it in my earlier comment but I was starting to wonder if I should include Google and Meta in that shortlist of legacy tech companies. Yeah, they're not that old relatively, but we're all getting older and they're well established at this point.

author: skybrian
text:
Some scenarios are worse than others. It’s not like anyone deliberately joins a startup that they think will fail, but it’s a possibility. A more pleasant one is that it starts growing and turns into a different kind of company.

Also, I’ve never actually started a job expecting to be there for more than a few years. It only happened once, at Google, and I switched teams a few times.

author: redwall_hp
text:
No, if anything a hypothetical drop in demand for skilled knowledge work would increase the labor pool of people for manual labor and drive the pay down even more.

Technical work pays more because a limited number of people can do it and it takes a large upfront investment in time to be able to do it professionally. Unskilled manual labor is something that anyone who's able-bodied can do.

Things like agriculture don't have more of an automation push because people are already paid next to nothing and developing the automation would cost more. Robots largely took over heavy manufacturing decades ago—it's largely large machinery building cars, for example. (Except for cheap commodities where it's cheaper to pay people in a heavily-outsourced area, like sewing shirts.) People do the dexterous in-between jobs, but that's the next big push. There's a reason why Hyundai/Boston Dynamics is working on hands for Atlas right now.

hypothetical drop in demand for skilled knowledge work would increase the labor pool of people for manual labor and drive the pay down even more.

author: redwall_hp
text:
Not voluntarily, but the hypothetical the AI zealots breathlessly advocate for is the complete destruction of virtually all knowledge work positions. That means people being forced to injure themselves doing those jobs for survival. (We're not magically getting a post-scarcity utopia from a group of techno-fascist billionaires.) Even a fraction of that population changing over would drastically increase supply of labor...and suppress demand, since there will be fewer people who can afford things like houses that need renovation, which would harm the trades even faster.

Of course, I would expect serious violence long before that point. There have to be at least a few unibombers among the population of <all office workers>.

Moreover, such a situation also would completely destroy the economy. If your main export is the product of knowledge workers, and you're racing to eliminate them for...something plenty of countries already have sufficiently replicated, well, good luck being able to afford to import all the things you don't manufacture (which building supply chains for is a pipe dream) when you've devalued your primary exports.

author: Bullmaestro
text:
The fewer people you have working for you, the fewer stock options you have to pay out, the less resistance there will be to watering down the product, collaborating with the military-industrial complex, or helping authoritarian governments control and murder their citizens. Over the past two decades, one of the more effective forces for keeping tech companies in line have been the tech workers themselves who have tried resist corrupt and unethical behaviour. It hasn’t always worked. There wasn’t enough of it. But what little there was it added meaningful friction at several important moments in tech history.


Have they though?

Fifteen years ago, the industry was desperate to hire coders. Landing a software engineering gig in a Big Tech firm was the dream. Their salaries were huge, their offices seemed luxurious and they were based in some of the most prestigious places in the world. And out of all of them, only Amazon really had a bad reputation for how they treated their workers pre-COVID (and it was really in their warehouse and logistics divisions.)

Since then it's been a race to shittify the entire industry.

author: creesch
text:
I have to agree here, not just towards their own working conditions but impact in general. I am in a different part of the world but it still surprises me that when I try to raise ethical concerns, or just concerns towards user impact that a majority of colleagues just sort of shrug and move on. Basically as long as they get to do fun technical stuff a lot of people in tech seem to be utterly blind towards the world around them and the impact they do or don't have. To be frank, I am seeing it in this thread and the photoshop clone thread as well.

You still see people en mass repeat the mantra of "technology is neutral" while ignoring that even if that is true the implementation certainly is not.

Two decades ago I do think we were in a better place as most of the behemoths we know today didn't have this iron clad grip on the industry just yet. Negative press actually might mean something and there was somewhat more meaningful competition. Once these companies become more established all of this started to matter less. At this point it is easy to see how management slowly started to realize how little pushback they'd get internally from more questionable policies.

In hindsight it is really easy to see how we ended up with an industry that is enshittified from both the in and outside.

author: arqalite
text:
I think the vast majority of us will have to try to shift towards more design/architecture-focused roles - i.e. not just being a programmer, but also a product lead, taking charge and driving decisions around the products that we develop, if we want to have a decent shot at remaining in the industry long-term. Lots of us (and I'm not saying I'm safe) will probably not make the cut, which is unfortunate.

If models keep getting better, companies will eventually flat out refuse to let us keep writing code by hand as models could output more of it faster, and our jobs will be prompting, reviewing, and dealing with the corporate tedium that models can't handle.

As much as I enjoy manual coding sessions, I can't deny that I can ship significantly more with LLMs than without them, so I've been picking and choosing my battles and dedicating the manual coding time to things I strongly care about.

At the same time, I'm considering trying to develop some products outside of my job and monetizing them as a side-gig; AI makes the time investment required a lot smaller, so I can justify spending a bit of my free time every day on them, and I'm confident enough in my QA skills to ensure a reasonable amount of quality. It's still a gamble, though, and I do need to find some good unexplored niches, which gets harder and harder as time goes on. But I'm definitely not banking on my job lasting forever so I need to find a solution that works for me.

author: Landhund
text:
I hope I interpret your "I feel like yapping about something related to this topic a bit more here" correctly as an invitation for well meaning discussion. If not, please don't pressured to respond (even though I hope do :) ).

Originally I planned to comment on most if not all of your points, but seeing as that would end up probably being almost as long as your blog post, I'll only comment on the first point.

But I want to assure you that I have read the entire post, spent plenty of time thinking about it and I very much appreciate you sharing your thoughts with us :)

Also, I hope I got this to sound as well meaning and in good faith as it is meant, but I wrote this to avoid having to deal with an annoying client, so hopefully no  hostility that truly wasn't meant for you hasn't bled through.

With that out of the way, here are my thoughts… (on only the very first chapter)


These companies literally stole the whole of internet and more. [...] If a normal person tried to steal this much shit they'd get jailed immediately.


My issue here is, people do get away with it? I just had a cursory look at r/datahoarder (simply because that’s the first places that came to mind), and the 4th highest post this year is a link to 300TB of scraped Spotify content. Also, the entire existence of Anna’s Archive and similar websites. And that’s just actually pirated content. Please don’t misunderstand me, I am in no way excusing those companies using pirated media/content, merely questioning whether what they are doing is actually unprecedented.

Which brings me to my next point: how does one steal the internet, specifically regarding all the public content? Because, well, it’s public, it’s openly available for anyone to see. Nobody needs my permission to take this comment or my own (very poorly written and not well maintained) blog and do whatever they want with it, except republish it. You could do a study looking at all the personal blogs out there, analysing the way they set up their footers or how they structure their links, etc., without needing their permission. Or I could go to the train station in my city with a clipboard and marking all the colors of all the jackets I see in order to… design a new jacket, I guess? That one kinda got away from me. Anyway, my point is, if something is publicly available, you don’t need permission to analyse it. If Google is allowed to scan books in order to index them and display snippets of them, I don’t see how scraping all of Reddit in order to analyse how people write is somehow not ok.

Another point I highly disagree with, is this:


its clear that these companies are building way too many data centers, way too fast [...] to meet some magical future hypothetical demand that just doesn't currently exist.


Funnily enough, I talked about this exact point with a close friend of mine just yesterday. Because the demand very clearly exists, right this moment. It’s why so many AI-Startups just die because of ever rising token costs. We are in a truly massive supply shortage of raw compute. Because LLMs effectively made raw computational power useful for any task that involves a computer of any kind. That’s why I truly don’t understand how the “AI Bubble” is supposed to burst. Because those datacenters will still be there. Because raw compute is now valuable. Because even if all those big evil AI companies (again not saying they aren’t evil, just that it doesn’t matter for this argument) go belly up tomorrow, open weight models will still be out there. GPUs and probably even specialized tensor processors will still be produced. Meaning that nothing is stopping anyone with some money to spare to keep tinkering with those models, trying to improve them, making them more efficient or better at specific tasks. Nothing is stopping my friend from using his newly bought 64GB RAM mini-PC to run 20T open weight models at 10 tokens per second for a week to see if it can spit out some digital prototype for his next new idea.

Yes, I agree that the current pace with which the big AI companies run through their money in order to train ever bigger models is definitely not sustainable. But it doesn’t need to be. Open weight models that I could run on my 5070 right now are already way beyond any threshold where I could see LLMs simply disappearing into obscurity. Deepseek and the like have continuously proven that what  is currently only possible with the most bleeding edge of proprietary models is not even a year away from being the mere baseline that any open weight model has to be able to provide.

author: Tygrak
text:
This is a blogpost (I guess? idk what to call it) that sort of tries to say that LLMs maybe aren't the worst thing ever created. If you are just tired of the infinite discourse about "ai", I completely understand not wanting to see anything more related to it, so to be honest just have a nice day and don't read it. I wrote it after arguing with people about LLMs too much online, which caused me to want to instead organize my thoughts about LLMs in some more productive way. It's probably way too long for the not very revolutionary points it brings. I am not a good writer, but I tried my best for quite a lot of hours to finish it, it probably still has a lot of issues but I could probably keep on rewriting it forever and maybe even just making it worse over time.

The article is as I said too long, but I feel like yapping about something related to this topic a bit more here, I am sorry. I sort of also thought that writing this article is something to do to make me feel like I did more for Timasomo than just make a Ludum Dare game in one weekend. And I am mentioning that because Ludum Dare also reminded me of being conflicted about LLMs too. Basically, the way LD is setup is that to get ratings on your own game you have to rate games other people made. That means I've been playing a lot of random games. Most games are basically the same as all the LDs I did before, some incredible, some... not so incredible. That is completely normal, and every LD I did was like that.

But then there were also a couple that were noticeably "ai" assisted. One didn't even bother to mention it anywhere, which just really annoyed me and made me refuse to play it. According to LD rules you should at minimum opt out of categories you didn't make by yourself, so if you didn't put substantial effort into making the art, or the music, you should opt out of the audio or graphics categories. But this person didn't care at all. And I just don't know what it is, is it that these people are actually just jackasses and always were jackasses? I've seen some people say that it really is "ai" itself that causes this. Anyway, that is alright, I saw 1 game fully slop vibed out with no respect for anyone out of many games, whatever.

The game that actually made me feel really conflicted is a game that I just played. It was honestly quite pretty, I liked quite a lot about it. It had a really good mood. The author of it disclosed that they used "ai" to create the engine for the game. I am ok with that. But where I started being confused is when I saw this middot character (this thing -> "·") in way too many places in the UI of the game. I feel like this thing is such an obvious tell of LLM written text and UIs. I feel like it's much more of a tell than for example em-dashes ever were, I definitely used to see some people use em-dashes normally even before LLMs were a thing. Meanwhile this middot thing I literally never saw anyone use in normal text, literally maybe like ever. Now it's everywhere in every vibecoded UI that exists. But the thing is that the UI and text in the game didn't really feel like stereotypical vibecoded stuff. But seeing that middot thing and also knowing that the author already disclosed they used LLMs elsewhere just made me start thinking about if other stuff might be LLM generated, or even just affected by LLMs. The only character in the game had a name that I feel like is basically what LLMs always pick by default as their very first choice when you ask them to suggest a name of a certain kind. Is it still perfectly plausible that the dev just picked that name? Yes it's definitely possible. In fact I think it's much more likely than that they asked a LLM to help them choose a name. But it just makes me really annoyed at myself that I am thinking about all this. I hate that I am by myself sort of going on this witch hunt in my head when I am playing this random game that I even feel like is one of the better ones I played in this game jam. The creator of the game really could have even used the middots, its not like it isn't a unicode character that exists for a long time, I am guessing someone even here on Tildes will tell me that they used to use it in normal text. And even if they did ask a LLM to help them pick out a name for a character, or even in general write the text, would it be that bad? I just don't know. I really don't know. I also don't really have any point where I am going with this.

author: RoyalHenOil
text:
I'm a frequent user of em dashes (as well as semicolons, etc.), and I've never used that dot symbol. I've rarely ever even seen it used, to the extent that I didn't recognize it at first and wondered if you were talking about bullet points. But then I remembered that Word uses that dot to represent spaces when you set it to markdown mode.

I wonder why LLMs like to latch onto certain obscure things so much.

Part of my day job involves editing text written by SMEs. Recently, some of the SMEs I work with have started using LLMs to help write the text, and I can very easily tell which parts the LLMs have written and which parts they wrote themselves. I still have to heavily edit both kinds of text; I'm just correcting different problems — more typos and grammatical errors with the human text (quick and easy to spot and fix), more structural issues with the generated text (more challenging to fix, especially since I'm not an expert on the subject matter myself). I hope it saves them time, because it sure doesn't save me any.

I've been using LLMs to help me edit, and I've found they also do much better editing human-written text than LLM-generated text. With editing human text, an LLM can halve the time it takes me to get through the work, but with editing LLM text, I can't tell that there's any time savings to be had. LLMs mostly don't notice the issues I'm seeing, and I have to hand-hold them through the process.

author: Akir
text: Ironically I had to use AI to understand what you were talking about. You used the acronym SME which is not common outside of your trade, and acronyms are famously difficult to figure out because anyone can use the same letters to represent anything. When I searched the most common meaning was Small to Medium Enterprise. Siri AI told me it was Subject Matter Experts. Is it right? Maybe not, but it makes a heck of a lot more sense.

author: blastedheath
text:
Did you write this?

I enjoyed it quite a bit and the points all resonate with my own lived experience. I've sadly become the "AI guy" in most of my social circles since I work at a tech company and have heavily embraced LLMs because I have to in order to survive in my career field. Plus I'll be honest, its a new technology, and the reason I got into this field is because I like learning about and using new technology. I'm far from a fanboy of the dominant players in the space or the way these things are created & run. But also - that doesn't mean they're not an incredibly useful tool when applied correctly.

It seems impossible to have a nuanced conversation about this topic since the (objectively bad) side effects and ownership model of LLMs make people so emotional. I like how you laid out each emotional reaction and then responded to it in a thoughtful and pragmatic way.

Your Photoshop example resonates with me. We've seen these immorally created tools used to immoral ends, but they don't have to be. Hopefully going forward we'll start to see the pendulum swing towards these tools empowering people to throw off the power structures that led to their immoral creation in the first place.

author: Wes
text:

I've never seen an LLM use one before, though, and I don't even know how you'd use them in conversational text.  I consider the middot a typographic tool, not a grammatical one.

author: raze2012
text:
, is it that these people are actually just jackasses and always were jackasses? I've seen some people say that it really is "ai" itself that causes this


"Always" is a strong word. But I'd say that this is simply the result of decades of broken windows. You spend a decade seeing trends of the worst, most obnoxious people being rewarded the most for their crude or outright malicious behavior, and that will affect your temperament. Maybe only in minor ways like "why do I need to return this shopping cart, anyway?", maybe in major ways in how you interact with and treat people.

Communities are contagious, in the best and worst ways.


I hate that I am by myself sort of going on this witch hunt in my head when I am playing this random game that I even feel like is one of the better ones I played in this game jam.


Well, I'm a game dev and I'd say I'm pretty anti-AI myself. But I do have to admit two things.




I have no clue how any competitive game jam is going to preserve its integrity. These are supposed to be timeboxed sessions of execution, and the one thing LLMs can do better is rapid prototype. I'm still very doubtful about full fledged releases, but a game jam isn't about that.




Despite the reverence for intellect and wisdom, modern society has always been at odds with enrichment vs. "content" production. And AI is putting us to the ultimate test on how much we value production over enrichment. And we're doing pretty terribly right now (for reasons related to the "environment" comments above).  We were doing terribly beforehand too, for the last 30ish years. But we're really diving off a cliff now.



Game jams are fundamentally supposed to be an environment of enrichment, so having suspicions on that being cheated for the sake of "production" is indeed a frustrating feeling.  It's like using a graphing calculator on a test about plotting graphs. It's not about the calculator  being good/bad, it's about robbing yourself of the learning process needed to understand graphing trends. But if someone does that and gets an A, there's that nagging feeling again. Am I here to learn or "produce" grades?

author: kacey
parent: (story) Qwen 3.8 27B on my laptop can interpret model weights, too
text:
As ruspaceni noted in the other thread, mixture of experts models -- such as Qwen 3.6 35 a3b -- work fine on relatively low amounts of VRAM by being able to efficiently spill out into system RAM. Before I blew $1300 Canadian loonies on an Arc Pro B70, I was running it on an RTX 2060 6gb card.

We've seen a few other, smaller shops train up MoE models that seem to be approaching the performance of some of Qwen's older, smaller models (e.g. Mellium2.1 12b seems to strike in the range of Qwen 3.5 9B, for instance), so it seems reasonable to assume that we'll see models that can run with less memory as time goes on. It's just that they fell out of vogue recently, presumably because the larger labs realized that they could court more favour with 100B+ models that compete directly with the present day frontier, rather than replicating performance from 6-12 months ago.
